tenement = an old multi-storey building divided into rented flats, often in a city centre
penthouse = a high-status flat on the top floor of a building, usually with a terrace
council housing = homes provided by the local authority at lower rent for people on low incomes
studio flat = a small flat in which the living room and bedroom share one space
bedsit = a single rented room used for both living and sleeping, with basic cooking facilities
high-rise block = a tall residential building with many floors of flats
tower block = a very tall block of flats, often associated with post-war housing estates
maisonette = a flat on two floors with its own internal stairs, usually in a larger building
loft conversion = an attic turned into extra living space
converted warehouse = a former industrial building turned into flats
period property = an older house with historic architectural features
thatched cottage = a small country house with a roof made of straw or reeds
farmhouse = the main house on a farm
hall of residence = a building of rooms for students, usually run by a university
shared accommodation = a flat or house in which unrelated people rent rooms together
sheltered housing = flats for elderly or vulnerable people with some on-site support
mobile home = a prefabricated dwelling that can be moved, often on a permanent site
prefabricated house = a house built from factory-made sections assembled on site
newly built property = a home that has just been constructed and not lived in before
second home = an additional property used for holidays or investment, not as a main residence
buy-to-let property = a home bought in order to rent it out rather than live in it
gated community = a residential area with controlled entrances and private security
housing estate = a planned area of houses or blocks built as a single development
brownfield site = previously developed land, often industrial, reused for new housing
greenfield site = land that has not been built on before, usually countryside or fields
terraced housing = a row of houses that share side walls with their neighbours
detached property = a house that stands alone and does not share walls with another dwelling
purpose-built flat = an apartment constructed as a flat from the start, not converted from a house
mixed-use development = a project combining housing with shops, offices or public services
residential development = a new group of houses or flats built by a developer
co-housing scheme = a community of private homes with shared facilities and joint decisions
granny flat = a small self-contained dwelling attached to or in the garden of a family house
basement flat = a flat partly or wholly below street level
attic flat = a flat on the top floor, often with sloping ceilings
garden flat = a ground-floor apartment with access to a garden
housing cooperative = an organisation whose members jointly own and manage their housing
open-plan = designed as one large space rather than separate rooms
underfloor heating = a system that warms a room through pipes or cables beneath the floor
fitted kitchen = a kitchen with cupboards and appliances built to fill the space
built-in wardrobe = a wardrobe constructed as part of the wall, not a free-standing piece
ensuite bathroom = a private bathroom attached to a bedroom
walk-in wardrobe = a small room used only for storing and organising clothes
conservatory = a glass room attached to a house, used for sitting and plants
cellar = an underground room used for storage, often cooler than the house
pantry = a small room or cupboard for storing food
mezzanine = an extra partial floor between two main storeys
skylight = a window set into the roof
bay window = a window that sticks out from the wall, creating an alcove inside
double glazing = windows with two layers of glass to reduce heat loss and noise
insulation = material that stops heat escaping from a building
boiler = the device that heats water for radiators and taps
fuse box = the panel that controls and protects a building's electrical circuits
extractor fan = a device that removes steam and cooking smells from a room
smoke detector = a device that sounds an alarm when it senses smoke
burglar alarm = a security system that sounds if someone breaks in
intercom = a speaker system used to let visitors into a building
parquet flooring = a floor made of small wooden blocks arranged in a pattern
laminate flooring = a factory-made floor covering that imitates wood
period features = original decorative details from the time a building was constructed
exposed brickwork = interior walls left as bare brick for a decorative industrial look
power shower = a shower with a pump that produces a strong flow of water
storage space = room in a home for keeping belongings
communal staircase = stairs shared by several flats in a building
fire escape = an external staircase or route for leaving a building during a fire
communal garden = outdoor space shared by residents of a block or estate
smart meter = a device that records energy use in real time and sends readings automatically
heat pump = a system that extracts heat from air or ground to warm a building
broadband connection = a fast internet service supplied to a home
damp-proof course = a barrier in a wall that stops moisture rising from the ground
cavity wall insulation = material pumped into the gap between two layers of an outside wall to keep heat in
airing cupboard = a warm cupboard, often around the hot-water tank, used to dry linen
breakfast bar = a high counter where people can sit and eat in the kitchen
kitchen island = a free-standing worktop in the middle of a kitchen
fitted appliances = fridges, ovens and similar machines built into kitchen units
walk-in shower = a shower area you enter without stepping over a high tray
wet room = a fully waterproofed bathroom in which the shower has no separate tray
amenities = useful facilities such as shops, parks, schools and clinics near a home
local amenities = everyday services available in the immediate neighbourhood
within walking distance = close enough to reach on foot in a reasonable time
well-connected = having convenient transport links to other places
poorly served by public transport = having few or unreliable buses and trains
green space = parks, squares and other vegetated public areas in a town
high street = the main shopping street of a town
cul-de-sac = a street closed at one end, with no through traffic
traffic congestion = too many vehicles on the roads, causing slow movement
cycle lane = a marked part of the road reserved for bicycles
pedestrianised zone = a street or area where cars are not allowed
refuse collection = the regular service that takes household rubbish away
commuter belt = towns and suburbs from which people travel daily to work in a city
dormitory town = a town whose residents mostly work elsewhere and return only to sleep
inner city = the central area of a city, often denser and sometimes poorer than the suburbs
leafy suburb = a quiet residential area outside the centre, with trees and gardens
rundown area = a neighbourhood in poor physical and social condition
up-and-coming area = a neighbourhood that is becoming more fashionable and expensive
rural idyll = an idealised picture of peaceful country life
urban lifestyle = the way of living associated with cities: density, services, noise and choice
pace of life = how fast or slow everyday living feels in a place
sense of community = the feeling that neighbours know and support one another
neighbourhood watch = a local scheme in which residents look out for crime and report it
next-door neighbour = the person living in the adjoining house or flat
keep yourself to yourself = to avoid social contact with neighbours and live privately
transport links = bus, rail and road connections from a place to other areas
catchment area = the zone around a school or hospital that determines who may use it
shopping precinct = a pedestrian area or small centre with a group of shops
street lighting = public lamps that make roads and pavements visible at night
isolated hamlet = a very small rural settlement far from towns and services
recreation ground = a public field used for sport and play
park-and-ride = a car park on the edge of a town from which buses take people into the centre
ring road = a main road that goes around a town rather than through its centre
convivial neighbourhood = an area where people are friendly and often spend time together
cultural facilities = places such as theatres, libraries and galleries in an area
healthcare facilities = clinics, hospitals and other medical services available locally
overcrowding = too many people living in a space that is too small
gentrification = the process by which wealthier people move in and prices push original residents out
homelessness = the condition of having no secure place to live
urban sprawl = the unplanned spread of a city into surrounding countryside
commuting from the suburbs = travelling daily from an outer residential area into the city for work or school
housing shortage = a lack of enough homes for the people who need them
soaring property prices = house and flat prices that are rising rapidly
unaffordable housing = homes that cost more than local people can reasonably pay
substandard housing = homes that are unsafe, unhealthy or below legal quality standards
rising damp = moisture that travels up walls from the ground, causing stains and decay
mould = a fungus that grows in damp rooms and can damage health
infestation = a large number of insects or vermin living in a building
noise pollution = harmful or annoying levels of sound in the environment
communal bin store = a shared place in a block where residents leave rubbish
vandalism = deliberate damage to property
antisocial behaviour = conduct that causes alarm, distress or nuisance to other people
derelict building = an empty structure in a very bad state of repair
vacant property = a house or flat that is empty and not being lived in
eviction = the legal process of forcing a tenant to leave a property
housing bubble = a period when property prices rise far above real value and then risk collapsing
negative equity = the situation in which a mortgage is larger than the home's market value
fuel poverty = being unable to afford adequate heating without cutting other essentials
sleeping rough = spending the night outdoors because you have no home
sofa-surfing = staying temporarily on friends' sofas because you have no home of your own
housing waiting list = an official queue for social or council housing
deprived area = a neighbourhood with high poverty and poor services
sink estate = a housing estate with severe social problems and a poor reputation
urban decay = the process by which buildings and public spaces in a city fall into neglect
regeneration = planned investment to improve a declining urban area
lack of privacy = the inability to be unseen or uninterrupted in your own home
thin walls = poorly insulated walls that let sound pass between homes
noisy neighbours = people living nearby who disturb others with loud sound
planning permission = official approval required before constructing or significantly altering a building
nimbyism = opposition to new housing or infrastructure near one's own home, while accepting it elsewhere
boundary dispute = a legal disagreement about where one property ends and another begins
house in multiple occupation = a property rented room by room to three or more unrelated people sharing facilities
mortgage = a long-term bank loan used to buy a home, secured on the property
deposit = a sum paid to a landlord as security, usually returned if the property is left in good condition
landlord = the person or company that owns a property and rents it to others
tenant = a person who pays rent to live in a property owned by someone else
landlady = a woman who owns a property and rents it to tenants
letting agency = a company that finds tenants and manages rented property for the owner
estate agent = a professional who markets homes for sale or rent and shows them to clients
tenancy agreement = the legal contract between landlord and tenant setting out the terms of the let
notice to quit = a formal warning that a tenancy will end
sitting tenant = a tenant already living in a property, often with strong legal protection
rent arrears = unpaid rent that a tenant owes
bills included = an arrangement in which utilities are covered by the rent rather than paid separately
council tax = a local tax on residential property that funds council services
stamp duty = a tax paid when buying a property above a certain price
conveyancing = the legal work of transferring ownership of a property
freehold = ownership of a building and the land it stands on, with no time limit
leasehold = ownership of a flat or house for a fixed number of years, not of the land itself
ground rent = an annual fee a leaseholder pays to the landowner
service lift = a lift in a building used for goods rather than residents
rent = the money a tenant pays regularly to live in a property they do not own
remortgage = to take out a new mortgage on a property you already own, often to get a better rate
equity = the portion of a property's value that you own, after subtracting the mortgage
first-time buyer = someone purchasing a home who has not owned one before
joint tenancy = an arrangement in which two or more people rent a property together on equal terms
guarantor = a person who legally agrees to pay the rent if the tenant does not
inventory = a detailed list of a property's contents and condition at the start of a tenancy
wear and tear = ordinary damage that happens through everyday use, not through negligence
housing association = a non-profit organisation that provides rented homes at below-market rates
sublet = to rent out a room or flat that you yourself are renting from a landlord
lodger = a person who rents a room in someone else's home, often sharing the kitchen
break clause = a term in a tenancy that allows either side to end the contract early after giving notice
energy performance certificate = an official rating of how energy-efficient a home is
